Anticline With a Soft Lens

A five-unit anticline carrying a low-impedance lens inside its middle unit, taken through every stage the tool actually performs — drawn geology, rock properties, the sampled numerical model, finite-difference propagation, CMP sorting, velocity analysis, stack and migration.

01

Draw the geology

The model is a symmetric anticline of five geological units, with a lens of soft rock sitting inside the middle one. Every boundary is a piecewise-linear curve through draggable control knees, so nothing here is hard-coded geometry — the same shape can be pulled around by hand afterwards.

One thing needs saying plainly, because it shapes everything downstream. The tool builds its subsurface from stacked bands: each layer owns a top boundary that spans the full model width. A lens is not that — it is a body inside a unit, confined in both directions. So the lens is built as a band whose top and base boundaries coincide outside its window. Where they touch, the band has zero thickness and vanishes; where they separate, the lens appears. That construction splits unit 3 into an upper and a lower band, which is why the two share a colour and identical properties: they are one limestone, and the sample below confirms the join between them is acoustically invisible.

Verified in the model

Lens thickness measured directly off the boundaries: 0 m at x = 260 m, 4.3 m at the window edge, 69.8 m at the crest, back to 0 m at x = 1040 m. All seven boundaries are monotonic across the whole model, and the lens top never rises within 74 m of unit 3's own top — it is genuinely embedded, not touching.

02

Assign rock properties

Each unit carries a P-wave velocity and a density. Their product is the acoustic impedance, and impedance is the only thing the acoustic solver actually cares about at a boundary: the normal-incidence reflection coefficient is R = (Z₂ − Z₁) / (Z₂ + Z₁).

The lens is deliberately slow and light — 2100 m/s against the limestone's 3400, and 2050 kg/m³ against 2500. That drops its impedance to roughly half the host's, which does two things at once: it produces the strongest reflection in the whole model, and it produces it with reversed polarity, because the wave is going from hard rock into soft rock.

Assigned properties. Impedance and reflection coefficients are computed, not entered.

The split unit is acoustically continuous

Because the upper and lower limestone bands have identical Vp and ρ, the reflection coefficient across the join between them is R = 0.000000, exactly. Away from the lens window the boundary carries no contrast and the vertical velocity function reports one continuous 220 m of 3400 m/s rock. The split is a bookkeeping device, not a geological interface.

03

Build the numerical model

The drawn boundaries are vector curves; the solver needs numbers on a grid. Every column of the model is evaluated independently and each cell is assigned the properties of whichever band contains it — 260 × 200 cells at 5 m spacing. This is where the geology stops being a drawing and becomes an array.

Two things worth noticing. The lens survives sampling cleanly because it is 70 m thick at the crest, or 14 cells — thin bodies below a couple of cells would alias away. And the grid the solver actually runs on is larger than the model you drew: a 90-cell absorbing halo wraps the left, right and bottom edges, so waves leaving the model are swallowed rather than reflected back as fake events. That halo is never shown in the interface.

04

Run the forward model

The forward model is a two-dimensional variable-density acoustic finite-difference simulation. A 35 Hz Ricker wavelet is injected just below the surface and the pressure field is stepped forward in time — 2057 steps of 0.4375 ms for a 0.9 s record, per shot. Nothing about the geology is assumed: reflections, transmissions, diffractions and multiples all emerge from the wave equation acting on the property grid built in the previous stage.

These four frames are a single shot at the crest of the structure, with the display gain compressed so weak energy stays visible alongside the direct wave.

05

The recorded shot gather

Each of the 40 receivers records the pressure at the surface for the whole record length. This is the raw product of the forward model — the first thing that resembles field data, and the last thing that is not yet processed.

Reflections appear as hyperbolas because the path from source to reflector to receiver grows with offset. The apex of each hyperbola sits at the zero-offset time of its reflector, and the curvature encodes the velocity above it. The whole of the rest of the workflow exists to exploit those two facts.

06

Sort into CMP gathers

Shot gathers are how the data is acquired; they are not how it is imaged. Each trace is re-filed by the surface midpoint between its source and receiver, and traces sharing a midpoint bin are grouped. With 20 m bins the survey yields 48 CMP gathers, the busiest carrying 26 traces.

The point of the sort is redundancy: a CMP gather holds several looks at the same subsurface point from different offsets. Averaging them will suppress what is not repeatable — but only after the offset-dependent time delay is removed, which is the next stage.

07

Velocity analysis and NMO

Flattening the hyperbolas requires knowing the velocity above each reflector. The semblance panel scans candidate velocities against zero-offset time and measures coherence, so a real reflection appears as a bright spot at its stacking velocity. Constant-velocity stack panels give the same answer a different way: stack the gather at a series of trial velocities and see which one focuses each event.

Applying normal moveout maps every sample from its arrival time back to the time it would have had at zero offset. Done with the right velocity, the hyperbolas become horizontal and the gather is ready to be averaged down to one trace.

A resolution constraint worth designing around

The lens top and base are 66 ms apart in two-way time — about 2.3 periods of a 35 Hz wavelet. That separation is deliberate. In an earlier version of this model unit 3 was thinner, putting the lens only 1.5 periods clear of the unit's own top and base; the four events tuned together and none of them could be picked reliably. Thickening unit 3 to 300 m fixed it. Resolution is a property of the model and the wavelet together, not of the processing.

08

Stack every CMP

Each corrected gather collapses to a single trace by averaging across live offsets, and the traces are hung side by side in midpoint order. 46 of the 48 bins meet the minimum-fold threshold. The result is the first image of the subsurface: the anticline is unmistakable, and the lens appears as a bright package near the crest.

But this section is unmigrated, and that matters. Stacking assumes each trace images the point directly beneath its midpoint, which is true only where reflectors are flat. On the dipping flanks of the anticline the real reflection point lies updip of the midpoint, so energy there is drawn in the wrong place.

09

Migrate

Migration moves the mispositioned energy back where it belongs. For every output point the section is summed along the diffraction curve a scatterer at that point would have produced; energy spread along that curve collapses to its apex, and dipping reflectors move updip. Here the whole 46-bin section migrates in about 380 ms with a 700 m aperture.

The comparison to make is with the third panel: the original model converted to vertical two-way time. That is the answer the processing is trying to recover, and it was never shown to the processing chain.

●

Connecting the geology to its signature

Reading structure off a section is one thing; showing that a specific rock body produced a specific wiggle is another. The cleanest test is to take the stacked trace from directly over the lens crest, take another from off the lens entirely, and compare both against the arrival times the model predicts.

Trace over the lens crest, CMP at 660 m. Predicted times come from the model's vertical two-way time; observed times are the largest wavelet lobe within ±0.4 of a period.

Lens top0.3688 s0.3763 s+7.5 ms−0.328− trough
Lens base0.4353 s0.4467 s+11.4 ms+0.328+ peak
Base unit 30.5030 s0.4957 s−7.3 ms+0.101− trough
Top unit 50.5830 s0.5797 s−3.3 ms+0.119+ peak

What holds up

Timing. Every event lands within ±11.4 ms of the time the model predicts — under half a wavelet period, which is about the precision with which a lobe can be picked out of an interfering wavelet train. The deviations scatter in both directions rather than drifting one way, so there is no systematic bias in the chain.

The lens signature. The lens top is a trough and its base is a peak. That reversal is the whole point: a wave crossing into rock of lower impedance reflects with inverted polarity, and crossing back out reflects normally. It is the classic soft-body signature, and here it can be traced back to two numbers a user typed in — 2100 m/s and 2050 kg/m³.

What to read carefully

Three honest caveats

Absolute polarity is not always a clean read. Four of the six events match the sign of their reflection coefficient; two of the weaker ones do not. Those two sit next to much stronger reflections, and the picked lobe is contaminated by a neighbour's sidelobe. The lens pair is reliable because both its events are strong and well separated — the relative flip between top and base is the robust observation, not the absolute sign of any single event.

Amplitude is not proportional to R. The lens has the largest reflection coefficient in the model but not the largest amplitude on the trace — the shallow top-of-unit-2 event is roughly five times stronger. Recorded amplitude also carries geometric spreading and transmission loss through everything above, neither of which R accounts for.

The unmigrated stack shows energy where no reflector exists. On the off-lens trace there is a substantial event near the time of the internal band join, even though that join carries R = 0 exactly. It is not a reflection from the join; it is dipping energy from the anticline flank drawn in the wrong place. That is precisely the artifact migration exists to remove, and a good reminder not to interpret an unmigrated section too literally.

Produced by driving the sandbox end to end — 18 shots simulated, 720 traces recorded, 48 CMP gathers sorted, 46 stacked and migrated. All 27 of the tool's built-in numerical checks passed throughout, and the run completed with no errors. Model, survey and processing settings are reproducible from the Anticline + soft lens preset.
